opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it still feels a little surreal to me. When I was a student, these people existed as names on PDFs. I'd be up late working through a paper on autoformalization or on neural theorem proving, scribbling in the margins and trying to reconstruct why they made a particular design choice. In a way they were my teachers long before I ever met them, through their writing.

Now they're sitting across the table from me, and we're arguing about the same kinds of questions I used to wonder about alone. I get to ask "why did you do it that way?" and hear the messy, honest version: the dead ends, the experiments that never made it into the paper, the intuitions they couldn't quite justify formally. That's the part you can never get from reading.

What I find most rewarding, though, is that it isn't just about meeting heroes. Many of these researchers came from different communities. Some were formal methods people, some were machine learning people, and some were mathematicians who cared deeply about proof. They didn't always talk to each other. At Axiom we're trying to build something that genuinely needs all of those perspectives at once. So watching someone who spent a decade in Lean sit down with someone who spent a decade on large-scale training and realize they're solving complementary halves of the same problem is really special.

There's also a sense of responsibility in it. When people whose work shaped how you think decide to bet their time on your vision, you can't take that lightly. It pushes me to be a better scientist and a better leader. I want to build a place where they can do the best work of their careers, maybe work that will someday be the papers the next generation of students stays up late reading.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest response directly.

You know, it's a strange and wonderful thing. When I was a student, these papers were how I learned to think. I'd sit with a result for days, trying to understand not just the proof but the taste behind it, why someone chose that formulation, what they were really after. The authors were names on a page to me, almost mythological.

And now some of those same people are sitting across the table from me, arguing about what we should build next. There's a moment I keep having where someone says something in a meeting and I realize, that's the exact intuition I absorbed from your paper years ago, and now I get to push back on it or build on it in real time. That's a kind of privilege that's hard to describe.

But honestly, the deeper reason it's rewarding is that these people don't normally get to work together. Mathematics is a very solitary tradition. You have collaborators, but mostly you're alone with a problem for years. At Axiom we're asking a question that no one can answer alone, which is whether machines can genuinely do mathematics, not pattern-match it, but reason, discover, prove. That requires formalization people, learning people, people who understand what a good conjecture even looks like. Putting them in one room creates conversations that simply wouldn't happen otherwise.

And I think there's a shared feeling among us that this is a moment in the history of mathematics, not just in the history of AI. So it's not just that I get to work with my heroes. It's that we all get to work on something that might change the thing we love.
